content: Once FDA approval is granted, a revised version of this guideline will be issued, replacing references to pending approval with statements confirming the approval. 3. All content in this publication is in the public domain and may be used or reprinted without permission, though proper citation of the source is appreciated. 4. References to non-CDC websites are provided for the convenience of readers and do not imply endorsement of these organizations or their programs by the CDC or the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 5. The CDC is not responsible for the content of external websites, and the listed URLs were accurate as of the publication date. 6. The use of trade names and commercial sources is solely for identification purposes and does not imply endorsement by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 7. CDC employees involved in the development of this guideline are named in U.S. government patents and patent applications related to methods for HIV prophylaxis. 8. Anticipating FDA approval of cabotegravir (CAB) for PrEP in late 2021, a new section has been added to address prescribing intramuscular CAB injections every two months for sexually active men, women, and transgender persons with indications for PrEP use. 9. A recommendation has been added to inform all sexually active adults and adolescents about PrEP (graded as IIIB). 10. 11. A table specific to CAB has been added, as CAB has a different dosing and follow-up schedule compared to oral PrEP, and does not require renal or lipid monitoring. 12. The determination of indications for PrEP use in sexually active persons has been simplified, and flow charts have replaced boxes for assessing indications in sexually active persons and those who inject drugs. 13. The HIV testing algorithm has been revised to include two separate algorithms: 14. F/TAF has been added as an FDA-approved option for sexually active men and transgender women at risk of HIV acquisition, though it is not approved for persons at risk through receptive vaginal sex, including cisgender women. 15. Sections on initiation and follow-up care have been revised and reordered to first describe guidelines applicable to all PrEP patients, followed by those specific to selected patients. 16. The frequency of assessing estimated creatinine clearance (eCrCl) has been revised to every 12 months for persons under 50 years of age or with eCrCl ≥90 mL/min at PrEP initiation, and every 6 months for all other patients. 17. Medications have been added to the table of drug interactions for TAF. 18. Options for PrEP initiation and follow-up care via telehealth (Tele-PrEP) have been outlined. 19. Procedures for providing or prescribing PrEP medications to selected patients on the same day as their initial evaluation (same-day PrEP) have been outlined. 20. Off-label prescription of TDF/FTC to men who have sex with men on a non-daily regimen (2-1-1) and their follow-up care have been outlined. 21. A brief section on primary care considerations for PrEP patients has been added. 22. A section on providing CAB for PrEP has been added. 23. The evidence review has been updated and moved to Appendix 2, with evidence reviews for CAB trials added. 24. Clinical trial results for transgender women and men who have sex with men (MSM) have been separated into distinct rows in evidence tables. 25. For more clinical advice about PrEP guidelines, clinicians can call the National Clinicians Consultation Center PrEPline or visit the CDC HIV website for resources. 26. Daily oral PrEP with emtricitabine (F) combined with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) has been shown to be safe and effective in reducing the risk of sexual HIV acquisition. 27. All sexually active adult and adolescent patients should receive information about PrEP. 28. 29. Daily oral PrEP with F/TAF is recommended for sexually active men and transgender women at substantial risk of HIV acquisition, but it is not recommended for women or others at risk through receptive vaginal sex due to lack of study data. 30. Renal function should be assessed at baseline for PrEP patients taking daily oral F/TDF or F/TAF and monitored periodically to prevent continued use in cases of significant renal dysfunction. 31. HIV infection must be excluded by symptom history and HIV testing immediately before prescribing any PrEP regimen. 32. HIV infection should be assessed at least every 3 months for patients taking daily oral PrEP and every 2 months for those receiving CAB injections to prevent continued use in cases of incident infection. 33. The two-drug regimens of F/TDF or F/TAF and the single-drug CAB are inadequate for established HIV infection and may lead to resistance if used in early HIV infection. 34. Clinicians prescribing PrEP should provide access to medication adherence support, additional risk-reduction services, and other effective prevention methods as indicated. 35. Dosage recommendations include daily oral doses of F/TDF or F/TAF with follow-up visits every 3 months for HIV testing, medication adherence support, and STI screening. 36. Follow-up care for patients on F/TAF should include weight, triglyceride, and cholesterol level assessments. 37. PrEP should be offered to sexually active adults and adolescents at substantial risk of HIV acquisition, with risk assessed through targeted sexual history and behavioral questions. 38. Gender-inclusive models of PrEP care are recommended to address the needs of all persons who could benefit from its use, including cisgender and transgender adults and adolescents. 39. Clinicians should routinely take a sexual history for all patients to identify those at risk of HIV acquisition and provide appropriate sexual health care. 40. Transgender persons should be considered for PrEP based on their risk of acquiring HIV sexually, even though clinical trials have not been conducted among transgender men. 41. Patients requesting PrEP should be offered it even if specific risk behaviors are not disclosed, as stigma may prevent open discussion of sexual or injection behaviors. 42. The guideline emphasizes equitable provision of PrEP to populations at highest risk of HIV acquisition, addressing disparities in access and use among Black, Hispanic/Latino persons, women, and residents of southern states.
